Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BANGKOK, Thailand (CNN) -- Demonstrators stormed a hotel Saturday where Asian leaders were to meet, forcing the indefinite postponement of the Association of South East Asian Nations summit. Thousands of anti-government protesters block a busy intersection during rush hour in Bangkok. Participating Asian leaders were on their way out of the country, according to Thai Prime Minister Abhisit Vejjajiva. He declared a state of emergency in Chonburi province and the southern coastal city of Pattaya, where the summit was to be held, but rescinded the order hours afterward. Thousands of "red shirt" protesters, named for the color of their attire, have rallied for days to demand Abhisit's resignation. The demonstrators flooded into the summit site after smashing through the hotel's glass doors, but were otherwise nonviolent. Hundreds of them streamed in, without police interference. Protesters hugged the officers and shook their hands. The red shirts have given the prime minister repeated deadlines to resign, but those have come and gone. United Nations Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon he was disappointed by the summit's delay. "I understand the circumstances that led the Thai government to take this difficult decision. While I had hoped to have exchanges with the leaders of ASEAN and its dialogue partners, I continue to look forward to engaging again with them in the near future," Ban said. "I strongly value the long-standing relationship between ASEAN and the United Nations, and their cooperation in various fields. I hope for an early restoration of normalcy in Thailand and for the settlement of differences through dialogue and peaceful means," he added. The protesters are loyal to former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra, who was ousted in a 2006 coup. Thaksin now lives outside of Thailand. The protesters have said Abhisit's government was not democratically elected and want him to resign and schedule elections. Abhisit, who has held the position for four months, has rejected calls for him to step down. Lawmakers named the 44-year-old, Oxford University-educated Abhisit prime minister in December in the wake of months of demonstrations against Thaksin and his ruling party, People Power Party. On Tuesday, protesters rushed Abhisit's motorcade while it was struck in traffic. He escaped unharmed. Protesters opposed to Thaksin took to the streets last year wearing yellow shirts, occupied the Government House and blockaded Bangkok's major international airport, stranding throngs of tourists who provide much of the country's revenue. The demonstrations ended in early December when a court ruled that the People Power Party was guilty of electoral fraud and threw Thaksin's brother-in-law out of the prime minister's seat. The red shirt protesters said this week they would not take over the airports. Dan Rivers and Kocha Olarn contributed to this report.

In Bangkok, thousands of anti-government demonstrators blocked a major intersection during the evening rush hour. Thai Prime Minister Abhisit Vejjajiva said participating Asian leaders were leaving the country. He imposed a state of emergency in Chonburi province and in the southern seaside city of Pattaya, the planned summit venue, but lifted the order several hours later.

For days, thousands of protesters known as “red shirts,” a reference to the color of their clothing, had been staging rallies demanding that Abhisit resign. Some demonstrators embraced officers and shook their hands.

The red shirts had repeatedly set deadlines for the prime minister to step down, but each passed without his resignation.

United Nations Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon said he was disappointed that the summit had been delayed.

“I understand the circumstances that led the Thai government to take this difficult decision. While I had hoped to have exchanges with the leaders of ASEAN and its dialogue partners, I continue to look forward to engaging again with them in the near future,” Ban said.

He added: “I strongly value the long-standing relationship between ASEAN and the United Nations, and their cooperation in various fields. I hope for an early restoration of normalcy in Thailand and for the settlement of differences through dialogue and peaceful means.”

The protesters support former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra, who was removed from power in a 2006 military coup and now lives abroad. They argue that Abhisit’s administration did not come to office through a democratic election, and they want him to resign and call new elections.

Abhisit, who had been prime minister for four months, has refused to step down. The 44-year-old Oxford University graduate was chosen by lawmakers in December after months of protests against Thaksin and his governing party, the People Power Party.

On Tuesday, demonstrators swarmed Abhisit’s motorcade while it was stuck in traffic, but he was not injured.

The previous year, anti-Thaksin protesters wearing yellow shirts held street demonstrations, occupied Government House and blocked Bangkok’s main international airport. The airport shutdown stranded large numbers of tourists, a key source of Thailand’s income. Those protests ended in early December after a court found the People Power Party guilty of election fraud and removed Thaksin’s brother-in-law from the premiership.

**Red Shirt protesters storm Thai summit venue, forcing ASEAN meeting postponement**

*PATTAYA, Thailand* — Anti-government protesters stormed a hotel hosting a major Asian regional summit in the Thai resort city of Pattaya on Saturday, forcing officials to postpone the gathering and evacuate several foreign leaders.

Thousands of demonstrators loyal to ousted former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra, known as the “Red Shirts,” broke through security lines and entered the Royal Cliff Beach Resort, where leaders from the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and partner countries were scheduled to meet.

The breach prompted Thai authorities to declare a state of emergency in Pattaya and cancel the summit, which was expected to bring together leaders from ASEAN nations as well as China, Japan, South Korea, India, Australia and New Zealand.

Television footage showed protesters pushing past police and soldiers, waving red flags and chanting slogans demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Abhisit Vejjajiva. Some demonstrators entered the hotel grounds and conference areas, while delegates and journalists were moved to secure locations.

Thai officials said the summit would be postponed indefinitely, citing security concerns. Several leaders were reportedly evacuated by helicopter or escorted from the venue under heavy guard.

The protesters accused Abhisit’s government of coming to power illegitimately after months of political turmoil and court rulings that removed previous pro-Thaksin administrations. They demanded fresh elections and said they would continue demonstrations until the government stepped down.

The incident marked a major embarrassment for Thailand, which had hoped to use the summit to project stability after years of political unrest. It also raised concerns among regional leaders about Thailand’s ability to host major international events safely.

The ASEAN summit had been expected to focus on the global economic downturn, regional trade and cooperation on security issues. Instead, the dramatic scenes in Pattaya underscored the depth of Thailand’s political divide between supporters and opponents of Thaksin, who was ousted in a 2006 military coup and later went into exile.

Abhisit condemned the protesters’ actions and said the government would restore order, while insisting it remained committed to democratic rule.

The Red Shirt movement, formally aligned with the United Front for Democracy Against Dictatorship, has drawn much of its support from rural northern and northeastern Thailand, where Thaksin remains popular because of his populist policies while in office.

Saturday’s disruption was one of the most serious challenges yet to Abhisit’s government and signaled that Thailand’s long-running political crisis was far from over.

**ASEAN Summit in Thailand Postponed Indefinitely After Protesters Storm Venue**

*PATTAYA, Thailand —* Thailand indefinitely postponed a major summit of Asian leaders on Saturday after anti-government protesters broke through security cordons and entered the hotel complex where the meeting was being held, forcing the evacuation of delegates and delivering another blow to the country’s political stability.

The summit, hosted in the seaside resort city of Pattaya, was to bring together leaders from the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and key regional partners, including China, Japan, South Korea, India, Australia and New Zealand. Instead, the gathering was abruptly abandoned after thousands of demonstrators loyal to ousted former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra pushed past police and soldiers and entered the conference site.

Thai officials declared a state of emergency in Pattaya and surrounding areas, while foreign leaders were escorted from the venue. Helicopters were used to evacuate some delegates from the hotel roof, according to Thai media reports.

Prime Minister Abhisit Vejjajiva, who had hoped the summit would showcase Thailand’s ability to lead the region after months of turmoil, said the meeting would be postponed indefinitely. He condemned the protesters’ actions and said the government’s priority was the safety of visiting leaders.

The demonstrators, known as “red shirts” for their signature clothing, accuse Abhisit’s government of coming to power illegitimately after court rulings and parliamentary maneuvering removed Thaksin-allied administrations. They have demanded Abhisit’s resignation and fresh elections.

Saturday’s disruption marked a dramatic escalation in a long-running political struggle that has divided Thailand between supporters and opponents of Thaksin, a billionaire-turned-politician who was ousted in a 2006 military coup. Thaksin remains popular among many rural and working-class voters who credit him with expanding health care, village loans and other populist programs. His critics accuse him of corruption, authoritarianism and undermining the monarchy, allegations he has denied.

The unrest follows months of street politics by rival movements. Last year, anti-Thaksin “yellow shirt” protesters from the People’s Alliance for Democracy occupied Government House and later seized Bangkok’s two main airports, stranding hundreds of thousands of travelers and severely damaging Thailand’s tourism-dependent economy. Those protests helped bring down a pro-Thaksin government after a court dissolved the ruling party.

Now the red shirts, formally associated with the United Front for Democracy Against Dictatorship, have taken to the streets in opposition to Abhisit’s administration, arguing that the political system has been manipulated by the military, courts and royalist establishment to block Thaksin’s allies from power.

The cancellation of the ASEAN summit is a significant embarrassment for Thailand and a setback for regional diplomacy. The meeting was expected to address the global financial crisis, trade cooperation and regional security issues. ASEAN, a 10-nation bloc that includes Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, the Philippines, Vietnam, Myanmar, Cambodia, Laos and Brunei, has often sought to present itself as a stable platform for economic integration and diplomatic coordination.

Instead, the images from Pattaya underscored Thailand’s deepening political paralysis. Although security forces were deployed around the summit venue, they were unable or unwilling to stop protesters from entering the hotel compound. The incident is likely to raise questions among Thailand’s neighbors about Bangkok’s capacity to host major international events while domestic tensions remain unresolved.

The government now faces the challenge of restoring order without provoking further unrest. Any heavy-handed response risks inflaming red shirt supporters, while inaction could deepen perceptions that the authorities have lost control.

For many Thais, the scenes in Pattaya recalled the airport occupations by the yellow shirts only months earlier — a sign that disruptive mass protest has become an increasingly common tool in the country’s political contest. With both camps claiming to defend democracy, and with elections, courts and street movements repeatedly reshaping governments, Thailand’s crisis shows little sign of ending soon.
